title: Dubai's Three-Michelin-Star Trèsind Lands in London — and Indian Fine Dining Will Never Be the Same
excerpt: Chef Himanshu Saini's celebrated Indian tasting-menu concept opens its first European outpost in Mayfair, marking a new milestone for Indian cuisine on the global stage.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Trèsind Mayfair opens as the first European outpost of Dubai's three-Michelin-star restaurant.
  • The restaurant features an eight-course tasting menu showcasing India's diverse regional flavors.
  • Indian fine dining is gaining global recognition, with new Michelin-starred restaurants opening worldwide.
  • Chef Himanshu Saini aims to elevate Indian cuisine to the same status as French and Japanese dining.
  • The restaurant's opening is significant for the 1.8 million Indian diaspora in the UK.
When Trèsind Studio in Dubai became the first Indian restaurant in the world to earn three Michelin stars in May 2025, it announced what many in the diaspora had long felt in their bones: Indian cuisine does not merely belong at the fine-dining table — it can lead it. Now, chef Himanshu Saini and the Passion F&B group have carried that ambition to London, opening Trèsind Mayfair on Hanover Street in the heart of the British capital's most prestigious dining quarter. The opening, on May 8, 2026, is being watched closely by chefs and restaurateurs on both sides of the Atlantic. For NRIs in the UK, it arrives at a moment when Indian food — long the country's favourite takeaway — is finally being treated with the same reverence once reserved for French and Japanese tasting menus. ## A Journey Through India, Course by Course Trèsind Mayfair operates as a tasting-menu-only destination, with an eight-course progression designed to take diners on a journey through India's regional flavours. Head chef Amit Bagyal, who previously helmed Yaatra, runs the London kitchen under Saini's creative direction. The experience opens with the restaurant's signature Chaat Trolley, an act of tableside theatre imported directly from Dubai. Three preparations — each tangy, crisp, layered, and startlingly inventive — arrive in quick succession, reimagining the street-food tradition as a fine-dining overture. Among the standout courses is the Khichdi of India, a dish that incorporates over 20 spices from different Indian states, each representing the flavour profile of its region. Other courses include a mushroom chai served tableside, tortellini filled with gorgonzola dolce on smoked chicken makhani, and lamb chops with rosemary vindaloo and chimichurri chutney — dishes that show how confidently Saini's cooking moves between Indian and European traditions without losing its identity. ## The Rise of Indian Fine Dining, Globally Trèsind's London arrival is part of a broader wave. In New York, Sujan Sarkar's Michelin-starred Indienne recently opened a second location in Hudson Yards, while Houston's Musaafer expanded to Tribeca. Mumbai's Masque, led by chef Varun Totlani, was named the best restaurant in India for the fifth consecutive year on the Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2026 list. "Trèsind began in Dubai in 2014 as my father's passion project — a modern interpretation of Indian cuisine rooted in creativity and hospitality," Suyash Nath, CEO of Passion F&B UK and US, told The Caterer. "Over the years, it has grown into a global story, and bringing it to London feels like a natural next chapter." The name itself — a blend of the French *très* ("very") and *Ind* (Indian) — captures the restaurant's ambition: to be emphatically, unapologetically Indian, while speaking the language of global fine dining. ## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 1.8 million people of Indian origin living in the UK, Trèsind's Mayfair address carries a particular charge. Indian restaurants have shaped British dining culture since the 1950s, but the narrative has been dominated by the curry-house model — abundant, affordable, often anonymous. A three-Michelin-star pedigree on Hanover Street rewrites that story. Chef Saini, who trained under Manish Mehrotra at Indian Accent in New Delhi before leading Masala Library and Farzi Cafe, has also released a companion cookbook, *The Rise of Indian Food: Recipes Reimagined by Trèsind Studio*, with a launch event at Fortnum & Mason. The basement bar, opening alongside the restaurant, draws on India's regional drinking traditions with cocktails made from lesser-known Indian ingredients and spices — extending the experience beyond the plate. ## What's Next Trèsind Mayfair opens for dinner only, Tuesday through Saturday. The tasting menu is priced competitively with Mayfair's Michelin-starred peers, though exact pricing for the London outpost has not been publicly confirmed. Reservations, already in high demand, are available through the restaurant's website. For a cuisine that has fed the world from street carts and home kitchens, a permanent address in Mayfair feels less like an arrival and more like a homecoming — to the table that was always set, waiting.
